  A Multi-Agent Perception-Action Alliance for Efficient Long Video Reasoning

           Yichang Xu1 , Gaowen Liu2 , Ramana Rao Kompella2 , Tiansheng Huang1 , Sihao Hu1
                     Fatih Ilhan1 , Selim Furkan Tekin1 , Zachary Yahn1 , Ling Liu1
                             1
                               Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA
                                          2
                                            Cisco Systems, USA
                             xuyichang@gatech.edu, {gaoliu,rkompell}@cisco.com,
         {sihaohu,thuang,filhan,stekin6,zachary.yahn}@gatech.edu, ling.liu@cc.gatech.edu



                         Abstract

This paper presents a multi-agent perception-action explo-
ration alliance, dubbed A4VL, for efficient long-video rea-
soning. A4VL operates in a multi-round perception-action
exploration loop with a selection of VLM agents. In each
round, the team of agents performs video question-answer
(VideoQA) via perception exploration followed by action
exploration. During perception exploration, each agent
learns to extract query-specific perception clue(s) from a
few sampled frames and performs clue-based alignment to
find the video block(s) that are most relevant to the query-
specific event. During action exploration, A4VL performs
video reasoning in three steps: (1) each agent produces
its initial answer with rational, (2) all agents collabora-
tively scores one another through cross-reviews and rele-
vance ranking, and (3) based on whether a satisfactory con-
sensus is reached, the decision is made either to start a new
round of perception-action deliberation by pruning (e.g., fil-
tering out the lowest performing agent) and re-staging (e.g.,
new-clue and matching block based perception-action ex-
ploration), or to conclude by producing its final answer. The
integration of the multi-agent alliance through multi-round       Figure 1. Responses from A4VL and three of the strongest closed-
perception-action exploration, coupled with event-driven          sourced models.
partitioning and cue-guided block alignment, enables A4VL
to effectively scale to real world long videos while preserv-
ing high quality video reasoning. Evaluation Results on five      Compared to traditional approaches [11, 14, 46, 56, 57, 59],
popular VideoQA benchmarks show that A4VL outperforms             MLLM-based methods [15–17, 33, 37, 38, 41, 49, 51, 53,
18 existing representative VLMs and 11 recent methods op-         54] exhibit strong ability for spatiotemporal visual reason-
timized for long-video reasoning, while achieving signifi-        ing, as well as human-level text understanding and gener-
cantly lower inference latency. Our code is released at           ation. However, most models often fail to produce high
https://github.com/git-disl/A4VL.                                 performance reasoning on long videos, because when the

   tuitively, perception exploration benefits from coarse, uni-
                                                                                           We presented A4VL, a training-free multi-agent framework
   formly distributed frames to cover the whole video, while
                                                                                           that tightly couples perception exploration with action ex-
   action exploration benefits from frames concentrated on ac-
                                                                                           ploration for long video question answering. By combin-
   tive events. From the table, we can also know the event-
                                                                                           ing event-aware block partitioning, clue-guided frame se-
   based partitioning only takes about 2 seconds.
                                                                                           lection, and multi-round agent alliance with consensus and
                                                                                           pruning, A4VL turns a pool of heterogeneous MLLMs into
   Table 5. Accuracy and latency of different sampling strategies on
   EgoSchema. R means random sampling and E means sampling                                 a coordinated reasoner over long videos under fixed com-
   from event-based blocks. The first character represents the sam-                        pute budgets. Across five different benchmarks, A4VL con-
   pling strategy for N1 perception frames, and the second character                       sistently improves over strong baselines and prior agent-
   represents the sampling strategy for N2 action frames.                                  based systems, and our round-level ablations show stable
                                                                                           gains from each collaboration round.
